question: How should the advance placement of warning signs be determined?
model_answer: Direct Answer: Advance placement of warning signs is determined by providing adequate Perception-Response Time (PRT) based on speed and the condition being warned of, using Table 2C-3 as a guide applied with engineering judgment. For temporary traffic control (TTC) zones, signs should be placed at distances varying by roadway type, condition, and posted speed — roughly 4–8 times the speed limit (in feet) on urban streets, 8–12 times on rural highways, and ½ mile or more on freeways and expressways — with Table 6B-1 giving recommended spacing. Guidance (recommended): - Where highway conditions permit, warning signs should be placed in advance of the transition and activity areas at varying distances depending on roadway type, condition, and posted speed; where a series of two or more advance warning signs is used, the closest sign should be approximately 100 feet for low-speed urban streets to 1,000 feet or more for freeways and expressways (Table 6B-1). - On freeways and expressways, advance warning sign placement should be longer because drivers are conditioned to uninterrupted flow, extending as far as ½ mile or more. - On urban streets, the effective placement of the nearest warning sign to the TTC zone, in feet, should range from 4 to 8 times the speed limit in mph, with the high end used when speeds are relatively high; the advance warning area should extend a greater distance when two or more signs are used on higher-speed streets. - On rural highways, the effective placement of the first warning sign in feet should be substantially longer — from 8 to 12 times the speed limit in mph — and the advance warning area should extend 1,500 feet or more for open highway conditions. - The effectiveness of the placement of warning signs should be periodically evaluated under both day and night conditions; Table 2C-3 provides guidelines for advance placement distance based on posted or 85th-percentile speed for Condition A (speed reduction and lane changing in heavy traffic) and Condition B (deceleration to a listed advisory speed). - Per Table 2C-3 notes, distances are adjusted for sign legibility (180 feet for Condition A; 250 feet for Condition B), and for warning signs with less than 6-inch legend or more than four words, a minimum of 100 feet should be added to the advance placement distance. Visual evidence: - [Image 1] Table 6B-1 shows recommended warning sign minimum spacing (dimensions A, B, C) by road type, ranging from 100 feet on low-speed urban streets to 1,000/1,500/2,640 feet on expressways/freeways. - [Image 2] Table 2C-3 shows advance placement distances by posted or 85th-percentile speed for Condition A and Condition B (e.g., 225 ft at 20 mph up to 1,600 ft at 85 mph for Condition A). - [Image 6] The full page view of Section 2C.04 shows the Guidance that warning signs should provide adequate PRT and that Table 2C-3 distances should be applied with engineering judgment. - [Image 8] The full page view of Chapter 6H (Section 6H.02) shows the Guidance on positioning advance warning signs in TTC zones with reference to Table 6B-1. Citations: - Section 6H.02 Guidance §1 (p.798) - Section 6B.04 Guidance §3 (p.771) - Section 6B.04 Guidance §4 (p.771) - Section 6B.04 Guidance §6 (p.771) - Section 2C.04 Guidance §5 (p.152) - Section 2C.04 Guidance §804 (p.153) - Table 6B-1 (p.773) - Table 2C-3 (p.152) - Page 839 - Page 812
gold_answer: Warning signs should be placed to provide adequate perception-response time. Table 2C-3 is an aid, but its distances should be applied with engineering judgment and can be adjusted for roadway features, other signing, and visibility.
